nameStory: The marsh meadow grasshopper gets its name from its favorite hangouts - the wet meadows and marshy grasslands where it thrives. The 'short-winged' part of its alternate name comes from its notably stubby wings that don't quite reach the tip of its body, making it look a bit like it's wearing a crop top!
description: The marsh meadow grasshopper is a small, brownish hopper that's perfectly at home in New England's wet meadows and grassy marshes. These compact little insects have a distinctive slanted face that gives them a somewhat serious expression, and wings that appear too short for their body. They're part of the short-horned grasshopper family, which means their antennae are relatively stubby compared to their long-horned cricket cousins. You'll typically find them hopping through tall grasses near water, where their brown coloration helps them blend in perfectly.

idTips.label: Slanted Face
idTips.description: The face slopes backward at a noticeable angle, creating a distinctive wedge-shaped profile that sets it apart from other grasshoppers

idTips.label: Short Wings
idTips.description: Wings are noticeably shorter than the body, stopping well before the tip of the abdomen - they feel papery and make a soft rustling sound when the grasshopper moves

idTips.label: Brown Coloration
idTips.description: Overall brownish appearance with subtle mottling that feels rough to the touch, perfectly matching dried grass stems

idTips.label: Compact Size
idTips.description: Small and stocky build that fits easily in your palm, with a solid, chunky feel when gently handled

idTips.label: Short Antennae
idTips.description: Antennae are thick and relatively short, feeling firm and segmented when touched, unlike the thread-like antennae of crickets

habitat: Look for marsh meadow grasshoppers in wet meadows, marshy grasslands, and along the edges of ponds and streams throughout New England. They prefer areas with tall, dense grasses and sedges where the soil stays consistently moist. You'll often find them sharing habitat with cattails, wild rice, and other water-loving plants in low-lying areas that flood seasonally.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, though they're still developing and may be harder to spot among the new grass growth.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity time when adults are fully developed, most vocal, and easiest to find hopping through tall marsh grasses during warm days.
seasonality.fall: Still active in early fall, though numbers begin declining as temperatures drop and they complete their reproductive cycle.
seasonality.winter: Adults die off with the first hard frosts, surviving the winter as eggs buried in the soil near water.

funFact: Despite having wings, marsh meadow grasshoppers are terrible fliers and rarely get more than a few inches off the ground - they're essentially the penguins of the grasshopper world, much better at hopping than flying!
confusionNotes: Often confused with other brown grasshoppers in wet areas, but the slanted face is your best clue - think of it as the grasshopper equivalent of a ski jump nose. If the face looks like it's leaning backward and the wings seem too small, you've found your marsh meadow grasshopper.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'short-horned grasshopper' refers to their antennae, not actual horns - it's an old way of distinguishing them from 'long-horned' grasshoppers (which are actually katydids and crickets). This can be confusing since we now know they're quite different families.
compareHints: Since this is the only Pseudochorthippus species in New England, compare it to other slant-faced grasshoppers in wet habitats. The marsh meadow grasshopper is typically smaller and more compact than most of its marsh-dwelling relatives, with proportionally shorter wings and a more pronounced facial slant. Its brown coloration is also more uniform and less striped than many similar species.
